title: Eco Warrior: Sort to Save the Planet
description: The Earth needs your help! Sort everyday waste items into the correct bins -- Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, or Compost. Learn how small choices make a big impact on our planet's health. Every correct sort reduces your carbon footprint!
learning_objectives: Understand the 4 pillars of sustainable waste management: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Compost
Identify which everyday items belong in which waste category
Learn how waste management reduces carbon footprint

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Read each waste item and its description carefully
Drag the item into the correct bin: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, or Compost
Earn 15 points for each correct sort, but lose 5 points for mistakes
Sort all items to complete the challenge and see your eco impact score
Review the explanations to learn why each item belongs in its category
tips: Reduce means avoiding the item altogether -- think 'Do I even need this?'
Reuse items can have a second life -- old jars become storage, torn clothes become rags
Organic and food waste always goes to Compost, while metals and paper go to Recycle

buckets.name: Reduce
buckets.description: Minimize usage -- avoid buying or consuming these items altogether to reduce waste at the source

buckets.name: Reuse
buckets.description: Repurpose items -- give them a second life instead of throwing them away

buckets.name: Recycle
buckets.description: Process into new materials -- send these to recycling plants where they become new products

buckets.name: Compost
buckets.description: Organic decomposition -- let nature break these down into nutrient-rich soil for plants

items.label: Single-use Plastic Bag
items.description: The thin plastic bags from grocery stores -- use cloth bags instead!
items.details: Single-use plastic bags are made from polyethylene, a petroleum-based material. They are used for an average of just 12 minutes but can persist in the environment for up to 1,000 years. India banned single-use plastics under 75 microns in 2022. Switching to reusable cloth or jute bags is one of the simplest and most impactful changes you can make.
items.fun_fact: India generates over 26,000 tonnes of plastic waste every day. If all the plastic bags used in India in a single day were laid end to end, they could wrap around the Earth multiple times!
items.environmental_impact: A single plastic bag takes 500 to 1,000 years to decompose. They clog drains causing urban flooding, kill marine animals that mistake them for food, and break down into harmful microplastics that enter our food chain and water supply.

items.label: Styrofoam Cup
items.description: Disposable cups from chai stalls -- bring your own reusable cup
items.details: Styrofoam (expanded polystyrene) cups are extremely lightweight yet nearly impossible to recycle economically. They are widely used at chai stalls, roadside eateries, and offices across India. Because they cannot biodegrade, they accumulate in landfills and waterways indefinitely. Carrying your own steel or ceramic cup eliminates this waste entirely.
items.fun_fact: Indians drink over 6 billion cups of chai every day! If even half of those are served in disposable cups, that is 3 billion cups going to waste daily. The traditional kulhad (clay cup) is a biodegradable alternative that has been used in India for centuries.
items.environmental_impact: Styrofoam is made from non-renewable fossil fuels and releases toxic chemicals when burned. It breaks into tiny pieces that pollute soil and water. A single styrofoam cup can take over 500 years to decompose, and it cannot be composted or meaningfully recycled.

items.label: Excess Packaging Material
items.description: Extra layers of plastic and thermocol in online deliveries
items.details: E-commerce packaging in India often uses multiple layers of plastic wrap, thermocol (Styrofoam), bubble wrap, and cardboard. Much of this packaging is excessive and unnecessary. Companies like Flipkart have started using paper-based packaging, but consumers can also help by choosing minimal-packaging options and consolidating orders to reduce deliveries.
items.fun_fact: India's e-commerce industry generates an estimated 1 billion shipments per year, producing roughly 2 lakh tonnes of packaging waste annually. Some startups in India are now making biodegradable packaging from mushroom mycelium and agricultural waste!
items.environmental_impact: Excess packaging wastes raw materials, energy used in manufacturing, and fuel used in transportation. Thermocol and plastic wraps are non-biodegradable and fill up landfills. Reducing packaging at the source is the most effective way to combat this growing waste problem.

items.label: Plastic Straw
items.description: Single-use straws from juice shops -- just sip directly or use bamboo straws
items.details: Plastic straws are among the top items found in ocean and beach cleanups worldwide. They are too small and lightweight to be recycled effectively and often slip through waste sorting systems. Alternatives include bamboo straws, steel straws, paper straws, or simply drinking directly from the glass -- which is the most sustainable option of all.
items.fun_fact: A viral video of a sea turtle with a plastic straw stuck in its nose sparked a global anti-straw movement. India banned single-use plastic straws as part of the 2022 Single Use Plastic ban. Bamboo straws made by tribal communities in northeast India have become a popular eco-friendly export!
items.environmental_impact: Plastic straws take up to 200 years to decompose. Due to their small size, they easily end up in rivers and oceans where marine animals ingest them. They fragment into microplastics that contaminate water and enter the food chain, ultimately reaching our plates.

items.label: Old Glass Pickle Jar
items.description: Amma's empty achaar jar -- perfect for storing spices or dal!
items.details: Glass jars from pickles, jams, and sauces are sturdy, food-safe, and easily cleaned for reuse. In Indian households, these jars have traditionally been repurposed to store spices, dal, sugar, homemade chutneys, and even as drinking glasses. Reusing glass jars avoids the energy-intensive process of recycling or manufacturing new containers.
items.fun_fact: Glass can be recycled endlessly without losing purity or quality, but reusing a glass jar is even better because it requires zero energy! In many Indian homes, the achaar (pickle) jar is passed down and refilled season after season, sometimes for decades.
items.environmental_impact: Manufacturing new glass requires heating raw materials like sand and soda ash to over 1,700 degrees Celsius, consuming significant energy and releasing CO2. By reusing a single glass jar just 10 times, you save the equivalent carbon emissions of driving a car for about 5 kilometres.

items.label: Torn Old T-Shirt
items.description: That faded cricket jersey -- great as a cleaning cloth or bag!
items.details: The fashion industry is one of the world's largest polluters. Old cotton T-shirts can be repurposed as cleaning rags, dusters, kitchen wipes, tote bags, or even braided into rugs. In India, the tradition of converting old saris and clothes into quilts (known as 'gudri' or 'kantha') has been practised for generations and is a brilliant example of textile reuse.
items.fun_fact: It takes about 2,700 litres of water to produce a single cotton T-shirt -- that is enough drinking water for one person for 2.5 years! India is the world's second-largest textile producer, and cities like Panipat are known as the 'cast-off capital' for recycling old textiles into blankets.
items.environmental_impact: Textiles in landfills release methane, a greenhouse gas 80 times more potent than CO2 over 20 years. Synthetic fabrics shed microplastics when they decompose. Reusing old clothes even once extends their life and halves their per-use environmental footprint.

items.label: Yesterday's Newspaper
items.description: The daily newspaper -- wrap gifts, line shelves, or make paper bags
items.details: Newspapers are one of the most versatile items for reuse. They can serve as gift wrapping paper, shelf liners, window cleaners, packing material, compost layers, or be folded into paper bags. In India, the raddiwala (scrap collector) tradition ensures newspapers are collected and given a second life, making India one of the best paper recycling ecosystems in the world.
items.fun_fact: India has over 100,000 registered newspapers and is the largest newspaper market in the world by circulation! The raddiwala network in Indian cities is an informal but remarkably efficient recycling system that has existed for over a century.
items.environmental_impact: Producing one tonne of fresh newsprint requires about 24 trees and 10,000 litres of water. By reusing newspapers before eventually recycling them, you extend their useful life and reduce demand for virgin paper production, helping preserve forests and save water.

items.label: Shoe Box
items.description: Sturdy cardboard box -- use it to organize stationery or craft supplies
items.details: Shoe boxes are made of sturdy cardboard designed to protect footwear, making them ideal for storage and organization. They can hold stationery, craft supplies, cables, small tools, jewellery, or keepsakes. Students can decorate them for school projects or use them as desk organizers. Their uniform shape makes them easy to stack and store neatly.
items.fun_fact: India's footwear industry produces over 2 billion pairs of shoes per year, making it the second-largest footwear producer in the world after China. That means billions of shoe boxes are generated annually -- reusing even a fraction of them would save tonnes of cardboard!
items.environmental_impact: While cardboard is recyclable, the recycling process still uses water and energy. Reusing a shoe box directly skips all of that processing. One reused shoe box saves approximately 1.5 kilowatt-hours of energy and 13 litres of water that would be needed for recycling and remanufacturing.

items.label: Aluminium Soda Can
items.description: Empty Thums Up or Pepsi can -- aluminium recycles infinitely!
items.details: Aluminium cans are one of the most recyclable materials on Earth. They can be melted down and reformed into new cans an unlimited number of times without any loss in quality. The recycling process uses only 5% of the energy required to produce aluminium from raw bauxite ore. In India, waste pickers and kabaddiwalas play a crucial role in collecting aluminium cans for recycling.
items.fun_fact: A recycled aluminium can returns to the store shelf as a brand-new can in as little as 60 days! India recycles nearly 80% of its aluminium scrap thanks to the informal waste collection network -- one of the highest rates globally.
items.environmental_impact: Mining bauxite ore for virgin aluminium causes deforestation, soil erosion, and water pollution. Recycling a single aluminium can saves enough energy to power a television for 3 hours. If India recycles all its aluminium cans, it could save millions of kilowatt-hours of electricity annually.

items.label: PET Water Bottle
items.description: Plastic water bottle with the recycling triangle symbol
items.details: PET (polyethylene terephthalate) is the type of plastic used in most water and soft drink bottles. It is identified by the recycling code '1' inside the triangle symbol on the bottle. PET can be recycled into polyester fibre for clothing, carpets, and even new bottles. India has a growing PET recycling industry, with facilities in cities like Chennai, Mumbai, and Delhi.
items.fun_fact: It takes about 5 recycled PET bottles to make enough polyester fibre for one T-shirt! India recycles about 90% of its PET bottles, thanks largely to the informal waste picker economy. Some Indian companies now make school bags and jackets entirely from recycled PET bottles.
items.environmental_impact: A PET bottle takes over 450 years to decompose in a landfill. Manufacturing PET from virgin materials consumes crude oil and releases greenhouse gases. Recycling PET reduces energy consumption by 60-75% compared to making new plastic from petroleum.

items.label: Amazon Delivery Box
items.description: Corrugated cardboard from online shopping -- flatten and recycle
items.details: Corrugated cardboard boxes are made of layered paper fibre that gives them strength and cushioning. After use, they should be flattened and kept dry for recycling. The paper fibres can be pulped and reformed into new cardboard about 5 to 7 times before they become too short to hold together. Always remove tape and labels before sending cardboard for recycling.
items.fun_fact: India's e-commerce boom has led to a massive increase in cardboard use. Flipkart, Amazon India, and other platforms ship millions of boxes daily. Many cardboard recycling units in India are in Punjab and Maharashtra, where old boxes get a new life as fresh packaging material.
items.environmental_impact: Recycling one tonne of cardboard saves approximately 17 trees, 26,500 litres of water, and 4,000 kWh of electricity. Cardboard in landfills generates methane as it decomposes. Recycling reduces landfill burden and preserves forests that absorb CO2.

items.label: Old Phone Charger
items.description: Broken USB cable -- e-waste recycling centres can recover metals from it
items.details: E-waste (electronic waste) includes discarded cables, chargers, phones, and other electronic devices. These contain valuable metals like copper, gold, and silver, as well as hazardous materials like lead and mercury. India has certified e-waste recycling centres where these items are safely dismantled and valuable materials are recovered. Never throw e-waste in regular dustbins.
items.fun_fact: India is the third-largest generator of e-waste in the world, producing over 3 million tonnes annually. A single tonne of discarded mobile phones contains more gold than a tonne of gold ore! Cities like Seelampur in Delhi have large informal e-waste processing hubs.
items.environmental_impact: Improperly disposed e-waste leaches toxic substances like lead, mercury, and cadmium into soil and groundwater, causing serious health and environmental damage. Proper e-waste recycling recovers precious metals, reduces mining demand, and prevents toxic chemicals from entering ecosystems.

items.label: Banana Peel
items.description: Left over from your morning fruit -- rich in potassium for soil
items.details: Banana peels are nutrient-rich organic waste that decompose quickly in compost. They are packed with potassium, phosphorus, and calcium -- essential nutrients for plant growth. Composting banana peels returns these nutrients to the soil instead of sending them to a landfill where they would produce methane. You can also bury them directly near plant roots for a nutrient boost.
items.fun_fact: India is the largest producer of bananas in the world, growing over 30 million tonnes annually! The states of Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Andhra Pradesh are the top banana producers. In some parts of India, dried banana peels are used as a natural fertilizer in home gardens.
items.environmental_impact: When banana peels end up in landfills, they decompose anaerobically (without oxygen) and produce methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Composting them aerobically at home produces zero methane and creates nutrient-rich humus that improves soil quality and reduces the need for chemical fertilizers.

items.label: Used Chai Tea Leaves
items.description: Leftover chai patti -- excellent for garden composting
items.details: Used tea leaves (chai patti) are slightly acidic and rich in nitrogen, making them an excellent addition to compost. They improve soil structure, attract beneficial earthworms, and help retain moisture. Tea leaves can be added directly to compost bins or spread around the base of acid-loving plants like roses, tomatoes, and ferns.
items.fun_fact: India is the second-largest producer of tea in the world and the largest consumer! Indians drink an estimated 837,000 tonnes of tea every year. The Assam and Darjeeling regions produce some of the world's most famous teas. All those used leaves could create mountains of rich compost!
items.environmental_impact: Used tea leaves sent to landfills contribute to methane emissions. But when composted, they act as a natural fertilizer and soil conditioner, reducing dependence on synthetic fertilizers whose production is energy-intensive and contributes to water pollution through agricultural runoff.

items.label: Eggshells from Breakfast
items.description: Crushed eggshells add calcium to compost and enrich soil
items.details: Eggshells are almost entirely made of calcium carbonate, the same compound found in limestone and chalk. When crushed and added to compost, they slowly release calcium into the soil, which strengthens plant cell walls and promotes healthy growth. They also help balance soil pH and can deter certain garden pests like slugs and snails.
items.fun_fact: India is the third-largest egg producer in the world, producing over 120 billion eggs per year! Andhra Pradesh alone contributes about 20% of India's total egg production. Finely ground eggshells can be used as a calcium supplement for plants -- they are essentially slow-release lime tablets for your garden!
items.environmental_impact: Eggshells in landfills are wasted calcium that could enrich soil. Composting them closes the nutrient loop -- calcium from eggs returns to the soil to help grow more food. This reduces demand for mined lime and synthetic calcium supplements used in agriculture.

items.label: Vegetable Peels & Scraps
items.description: Potato skins, onion peels, carrot tops from cooking dinner
items.details: Vegetable peels, stems, roots, and trimmings from daily cooking are ideal for composting. These green (nitrogen-rich) materials decompose quickly and form the base of high-quality compost. Common Indian kitchen scraps like potato peels, onion skins, carrot tops, palak stems, and gourd seeds are all compostable. Layer them with dry brown materials like leaves or newspaper for best results.
items.fun_fact: Indian households waste nearly 68.7 million tonnes of food per year, according to a UN report -- the highest of any country. A significant portion of this is vegetable and fruit scraps that could be composted. Cities like Bengaluru and Pune have pioneered community composting programs to tackle this problem.
items.environmental_impact: Food waste in landfills is the third-largest source of methane emissions globally. Composting vegetable scraps at home can divert up to 30% of household waste from landfills. The resulting compost enriches soil, retains water, and reduces the need for chemical fertilizers, creating a virtuous cycle of sustainability.

win_conditions.description: Sort all 16 waste items into the correct sustainability bins! Fewer mistakes = higher Eco Score. Become a true Eco Warrior!

glossary_terms.definition: The mental effort required to process information and make decisions.
glossary_terms.example: Having too many options at once makes decisions harder and slower.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Working memory has limits. Experts chunk information into patterns, reducing cognitive load and enabling faster decisions.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Experienced doctors diagnose faster not because they think harder, but because they recognize patterns instantly.

glossary_terms.definition: Identifying recurring structures or relationships in information.
glossary_terms.example: Noticing that certain question types always have two plausible answers helps you focus faster.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Pattern recognition is a core skill in chess, medicine, engineering, and sport. It develops through deliberate practice.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Air traffic controllers recognize dangerous flight patterns faster than computers because of years of pattern training.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to direct mental attention toward what matters most and ignore distractions.
glossary_terms.example: Under time pressure, completing questions you're confident about before tackling harder ones.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Focus is a trainable skill. The Pomodoro method, mindfulness, and deliberate practice all improve sustained attention.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Olympic athletes train mental focus as rigorously as physical skills — pressure performance depends on it.

coaching_moment: If you get something wrong, reset and continue. Resilience isn't about never failing — it's about how quickly you get back on track.
cultural_context: India is among the world's most climate-vulnerable nations. Environmental thinking is increasingly integrated into India's school curricula under NEP 2020, preparing students for the sustainability challenges of India's development.
reflection_prompt: What pattern did you start to recognize as you played? How will you use it next time?
